title: Adab of speech
hook: say good or keep silent: the manners of the tongue start in the gap before a word

segments.voice: Yesterday, adab: courtesy toward Allah, toward people, toward things. Your line was courtesy in everything. What was the one thing you did courteously? Today adab moves to the place it gets tested fastest: the mouth. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-two.

A reply sits half typed. The cursor blinks. It's sharp, it's accurate, and it would land. Your thumb hovers over send. Between the thought and the word there's a gap about the width of one breath, and a great deal happens in that gap. The manners of speech in Islam begin right there, with a short line from the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. It ties the way a person talks to faith itself. And it offers exactly two choices. Neither of them is the sharp reply.
screen: `A REPLY, HALF TYPED.` → `THE GAP OF ONE BREATH.` → `TWO CHOICES.`

segments.voice: The hadith is in Sahih al-Bukhari. In paraphrase: whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him say what is good, or keep silent. Notice how it's built. It doesn't open with a rule about words. It opens with belief, as if speech is where faith shows up in public. Then it gives two doors, and only two. Good, or silent. There's no third door marked true, so I'll say it anyway. The Qur'an raises the bar in its own words. In al-Isra, in Pickthall's translation: "Tell My bondmen to speak that which is kindlier." Not only kind. Kindlier. Of two true things you could say, the gentler one. And in al-Baqarah, among the duties of a covenant: "speak kindly to mankind." Mankind, not only friends. The Qur'an also says that words don't simply vanish. Surah Qaf says of each person: "He uttereth no word but there is with him an observer ready." Tradition says that observer is an angel who records. Some readers take the verse less as a threat than as a reason to slow down. A few days ago this path looked at backbiting and lying. Today is the filter that comes before both. And one more turn, so the hadith isn't misheard. Silence here doesn't mean swallowing the truth when it's needed. The Qur'an also calls believers to stand firm for justice, as witnesses for Allah, even against themselves. The silence of the hadith is a chosen silence: the word you could have said, left unsaid, because it wasn't good. It's courtesy, held in the mouth.
screen: `SAY GOOD, OR KEEP SILENT.` · `FAITH SHOWS UP IN SPEECH.` · `SPEAK THAT WHICH IS KINDLIER.` · `SILENCE AS A CHOICE, NOT A HIDING.`

segments.voice: The practice: pause before speaking. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one conversation coming up today, or one message waiting for a reply. Hear the first thing you'd say. Now hold it at the two doors. Is it good? If it isn't, can it become kindlier, or can it stay unsaid? Don't decide for the whole day. Just practice the gap. Breathe in, notice the word. Breathe out, and let it wait. If you pray, you can hold the words speak that which is kindlier in the quiet. The bell holds the time.
Adab of speech. The manners of the tongue: say what is good or keep silent, and of two true words, choose the kindlier. Today's word.
Your line: good, or silent. Today, before one reply, take one breath first, and let the two doors decide what goes through. Tomorrow, the adab of eating. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: Muslim teachers cite the hadith "say good or keep silent" when they teach the manners of speech, often alongside the Qur'an's call to speak the kindlier word.

myth: the hadith opens with a rule about words

the Qur'an asks for the kindlier word, not only a true one
al-Isra: tell My bondmen to speak that which is kindlier.
keeping silent means never speaking up

fork.setup: a friend shares something they're proud of. you spot a flaw and have a sharp, accurate comment ready. by today's hadith, what are your doors?
options: the sharp comment, because it's true.
say it to someone else instead.
fork.reveal: the hadith gives two doors only: say what is good, or keep silent. true, so I'll say it anyway isn't one of them.

original.note: Arabic: "let him keep silent," the hadith's second door.

trapdoor: what you thought: the adab of speech means not swearing.
what it means: a filter before every word: say good or keep silent, and choose the kindlier of two true things.
what a scholar hears: a hadith that ties speech to belief in Allah and the Last Day, in the same breath as honoring the neighbor and the guest.
